name: Brow microshading / powder brows

lead: Microshading or powder brows is a cosmetic tattoo that fills the brows with a soft, makeup-like gradient instead of drawn hairs. It is offered at tattoo and beauty studios.
The sources reviewed describe brow tattooing generally rather than this technique specifically, so published evidence on it by name is thin.

paras: A technician deposits pigment, commonly iron-oxide based, into the skin to create a shaded brow shape. Results fade gradually and touch-ups are typically recommended.
Reported risks include allergic reactions, infection, granulomas, keloids and pigment migration, and removal can be hard. Regulation varies; in the US there is no federal technician standard.

lead: Brow microshading, also marketed as powder brows or ombre brows, is a form of cosmetic eyebrow tattooing intended to give a soft, filled-in, makeup-like finish rather than individual hair-like strokes. It belongs to the wider field of permanent makeup, in which pigment is deposited in the dermis.[1]

The sources reviewed for this article describe eyebrow tattooing in general but do not describe microshading or powder brows by name. Reference works report that cosmetic brow tattoos fade over time, can usually be removed only with difficulty, and carry risks including allergic reactions, infection, granulomas and pigment migration.[1][2]
infobox: No federal technician standard; FDA treats inks as cosmetics

paras: Permanent makeup uses tattooing to place pigment in the dermis, and is used for eyeliner, lip color and eyebrows, including for people who have lost brow hair through aging, illness, chemotherapy or genetic conditions.[1] Microblading, a related eyebrow technique, uses a handheld tool to draw hair-like strokes, whereas microshading and powder brows are marketed as producing a stippled or gradient fill; the sources reviewed do not describe the latter methods in detail.[2]

Brow tattoos fade with sun exposure, skin type, products and medications, and microblading-type treatments are reported to last up to about two years, with touch-ups often recommended after about six weeks and then every 12 to 18 months.[2] Permanent makeup removal can be difficult or sometimes impossible; options include laser, dermabrasion, surgical excision and chemical removal.[1]

Common short-term effects include itching, redness and swelling. Less common complications include allergic reactions, infection, granulomas, keloids and, rarely, swelling or burning during MRI scans linked to some pigments.[1] Unsterilized equipment can transmit bloodborne infections.[1][2]

In the United States the FDA reviews inks as cosmetics, some pigments are not approved for skin use, and technician requirements vary by state.[1] In Canada microblading is regulated as a personal service by individual provinces.[2]

timeline.event: British tattoo artist Sutherland MacDonald is the earliest well-documented permanent-makeup practitioner, working in London.[1]
Cosmetic eyebrow tattooing becomes more common in the US and Asia.[2]
Microblading becomes popular in the US and Canada.[2]
